newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli bonds end higher on interest rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Israeli bonds end higher on interest rate cut.

text.p: Israeli bonds closed higher on Wednesday after a cut in the central bank's key lending rate boosted demand, traders said.
Indices:
* Government bonds general: +0.34 pct to 107.47
* CPI-linked government bonds: +0.31 pct to 107.26
* Unlinked government bonds: +0.41 pct to 108.95
* Dollar-linked government bonds: +0.45 pct to 105.93
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.18 pct to 106.87
Volume including Makams was 123 million shekels, of which a high 30 million was for dollar-linked bonds.

"Today was a special day, after the storm yesterday and the new economic programme," said Adam Reuter of Financial Immunities consultancy. "There was demand for all kinds of bonds because of expectations of a cut in interest rates which was implemented."

After the Israeli cabinet adopted a plan to widen the exchange rate band, the central bank said on Wednesday it would reduce its key lending rate by 1.2 percentage points to 12.7 percent, effective Thursday. It was the first rate cut since February.
Unlinked bonds had the highest price rises, with yields ranging between 13.3 to 13.8. Yields on Makams for one year reached 12.5 percent, traders said.
"CPI-linked long bonds also registered dramatic rises of 0.4 to 0.5 percent on the lower interest rate," said Reuter, while short-term CPI-linked bonds were stable with a positive trend.
Prices of dollar-linked bonds, which had been falling because of the rumours of an expansion of the shekel's trading band, rose on Wednesday.
Reuter attributed the rise to attractive yields of seven percent and the feeling that lower shekel interest rates would make dollar-linked bonds more popular.
The shekel representative rate was fixed slightly lower against the dollar on Wednesday in very volatile trading following the cabinet's approval of the foreign exchange reform.

"Yields on CPI-linked long bonds are now around four percent," said Zion Nimrod of Nesuah Trading and Investment. "This was a first reaction to the interest rate cut. I think these bonds have found a balance at this level."
The shekel has been allowed to trade in a band of seven percent above or below a diagonal slope designed to devalue the Israeli currency by six percent a year.
But high interest rates have buoyed the shekel, forcing the Bank of Israel to buy massive amounts of dollars to prevent the shekel from strengthening beyond its band.

Under the new plan the lower band remains the same while the upper band rises to 21 percent. The spread between the top and bottom band, therefore, will be 28 percent. The central bank hopes this will eliminate the need to intervene constantly in the currency market.
Israeli Finance Minister Dan Meridor quit on Wednesday in a tiff with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after the cabinet adopted the plan.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with durations of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
($1 = 3.42 shekels)
-- Shoshanna Solomon, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 x233
